resolution: Three senses. Aptitude (DEF-TRUTH-VALUE, O'Connor's `TruthApt`): being the kind of sentence that can be true or false, in the robust sense of DEF-TRUTH-ROBUST. Having a truth value in fact (DEF-THOUGHT-TRUE-OR-FALSE, `TrueT t ∨ FalseT t`): the sense of Metaphysics IV.7, reading A. STMT-TRUTH-APT-THOUGHT-AFFIRMS-OR-DENIES and STMT-TRUTH-APT-THOUGHT-DECIDES-ITS-OBJECT are about thoughts true or false in fact, so their conclusion excludes no third thought that is merely apt. No step passes from aptitude to having a truth value: bivalence, that every object of thought is judged truly or falsely, is the separate explicit premise STMT-EVERY-OBJECT-OF-THOUGHT-JUDGED-TRULY-OR-FALSELY (reading B), and ARIST-MET-1012A-THOUGHT-BIVALENCE-IFF-EXCLUDED-MIDDLE shows it is equivalent to excluded middle rather than assuming it. Minimal aptness (DEF-MINIMAL-TRUTH-APTNESS, the `TruthApt` of the van Roojen readings, #185 and #190): truth-apt in the deflationary sense only. It is a different Lean parameter from O'Connor's `TruthApt`, and in the van Roojen readings robust aptness is the separate predicate `RobustlyTruthApt` (DEF-TRUTH-ROBUST), so no step passes from minimal to robust aptness silently. The only bridge between them is the explicit, open collapse premise STMT-NO-ROBUST-TRUTH-APTNESS-BEYOND-MINIMAL: the collapse argument on the robust-truth deviation assumes it, and the anti-realist argument on the same deviation denies it from other open premises.
